blocks.content: I've kept sketchbooks since I was twelve. Forty-three of them now. My mom has the early ones in a bin in her closet and I found them once looking for my rain jacket and spent forty minutes on the floor reading my own handwriting from when I was fourteen. The drawings were bad. The notes I'd written to myself in the margins were more interesting. Even then I was writing things down about light.

The way I start a drawing: loose shapes first. No detail yet, just the feeling of the thing. The outline of the street, the suggestion of the awning, the rough geometry of the buildings. I don't go specific until I understand what I'm actually looking at. Detail too early is just guessing.
The street outside was doing something good with the morning. The bakery awning, the bookstore sign, the woman with yellow flowers moving along the sidewalk. I drew all of it loose, just marks.
My hand went there on its own. I redirected it once. Then again. The third time I let it go.
I told myself I was practicing figures. Which is true — figure drawing is a real thing, a necessary thing. I told myself that clearly and directly.
